# Transcaval Access for Structural Heart Interventions: A Narrative Review

## Introduction

Transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) has transformed the management of aortic stenosis across the surgical-risk spectrum, with outcomes comparable to surgery in intermediate-risk patients. In intermediate-risk patients with severe symptomatic aortic stenosis, surgical and transcatheter valve replacement were similar with respect to the primary end point of death or disabling stroke for up to 2 years [1]. The transfemoral artery is the preferred and least invasive route, but a subset of patients have anatomical or clinical factors precluding this approach [2]. Approximately 5–10% of candidates are unsuitable owing to small caliber, tortuosity, or heavy calcification of the iliofemoral vessels [3]. Historically, such patients underwent transthoracic (transapical or transaortic) access, but transthoracic access is inferior compared with femoral artery access, and discomfort and morbidity are more pronounced, probably because of the invasiveness and pulmonary insults [4].

## Concept and Rationale

Transcaval access offers a fully percutaneous alternative. Transcaval access is a fully-percutaneous catheter route from the inferior vena cava, across the retroperitoneal interstitial space, and into the abdominal aorta to enable therapeutic procedures such as transcatheter aortic valve replacement [5]. The technique was first validated in swine, demonstrating that large therapeutic devices can be introduced into the aorta via the IVC in a simple catheter procedure, and the fistula closed uneventfully despite full anticoagulation, with intentional failure to close the tract being well-tolerated and easily redressed [6]. Its counterintuitive safety rests on a hemodynamic principle: although counterintuitive, its relative safety derives from the recognition that interstitial hydraulic pressure exceeds venous pressure, so arterial bleeding harmlessly decompresses into the nearby caval venous hole [7].

## Technique

The procedure relies on transcatheter electrosurgery. Transcatheter electrosurgery uses continuous duty-cycle radiofrequency energy to vaporize and therefore traverse or lacerate tissue [8]. From the femoral vein, an electrified guidewire is directed from the inferior vena cava into a snare prepositioned in the adjoining abdominal aorta [9]. After delivering a microcatheter to exchange for a stiff guidewire, the transcatheter heart valve introducer sheath is advanced from the femoral vein into the abdominal aorta for conventional transfemoral retrograde TAVR [10]. At completion, the resulting aorto-caval fistula is closed with a nitinol cardiac occluder device [11]. A step-by-step procedural guide has been published to facilitate adoption [12].

## Patient Selection and Imaging

Careful CT planning is essential. The target must have a calcium-free window on the right wall of the abdominal aorta, close to the vena cava, free of interposed structures such as bowel or lymph nodes, and away from branches that could be obstructed by a closure device [13]. A dedicated CT-based methodology and anatomic suitability classification have been developed to standardize candidate selection [14,15].

## Clinical Evidence

The first-in-human series established proof of concept: feasibility of venous access to the aorta to allow TAVR in otherwise ineligible patients was demonstrated, challenging conventional wisdom about intentionally violating the wall of the aorta [16]. The prospective NHLBI investigation confirmed that transcaval access may enable fully percutaneous TAVR without the hazards and discomfort of transthoracic access [17]. At one year, there were no late vascular complications of transcaval access; 93% of fistulas were proven occluded at last follow-up, and only one was proven patent after 12 months [18].

The European multicentre registry reported reassuring early results: transcaval access was successful in 49 of 50 patients and device success was obtained in 94% of cases; closure with a nitinol cardiac occluder was successful in all cases without need for emergent surgery [19]. A single-center comparison found that length of hospital stay for transcaval patients was significantly shorter than for alternative-access patients [20]. In a multicenter U.S. analysis, transcaval access had a lower rate of stroke/TIA than transaxillary access, comparable bleeding and vascular complications, and a higher rate of discharge directly to home [21]. A systematic review and meta-analysis concluded that the transcaval approach is increasingly used in TAVR in patients unsuitable for the gold-standard transfemoral approach, supporting its safety and efficacy [22].

## Other Applications

Beyond TAVR, transcaval access has broadened to other large-bore interventions. It has been applied to thoracic endovascular aortic repair, in lieu of a surgical iliac conduit when pelvic arteries are small and atherosclerotic [23]. It also enables mechanical circulatory support: transcaval access is feasible for emergency nonsurgical implantation of the Impella 5.0 device in cardiogenic shock with small or diseased iliofemoral arteries [24]. It has further been used across surgical grafts [25] and to facilitate subaortic and congenital interventions [26,27].

## Limitations and Future Directions

A key barrier remains device availability. The dissemination of transcaval access and closure techniques has been hampered by the unavailability of commercially marketed devices [28]. Closure currently relies on off-label nitinol occluders, and dedicated closure devices may further reduce the incidence of bleeding after transcaval access [21]. Encouragingly, transcaval access techniques can be disseminated through training and proctorship [21]. Current guidance suggests that institution-specific structural heart teams should focus on gaining proficiency in 1 or 2 alternative access techniques [2,29]. Foundational preclinical and registry work continues to support expanded use [30].

## Conclusion

Transcaval access has matured from a daring concept into a validated, fully percutaneous strategy for patients lacking transfemoral options. With favorable comparative outcomes and growing applications beyond TAVR, its broader adoption awaits dedicated closure devices and continued operator training.
